strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: measuring text-image alignment during the reverse diffusion process rather than post-hoc, with a clear practical motivation (early stopping / mid-generation BoN selection to save compute).

Provides a useful community resource: two released benchmark datasets (Noisy-Conceptual-Captions, Noisy-GenAI-Bench with stored intermediate latents) that fill a real gap, since no open datasets of intermediate noise sequences previously existed; this enables reproducible comparison.

The experimental program is reasonably comprehensive: BoN cost/quality trade-off analysis, factual consistency with systematically corrupted prompts (well-designed four corruption dimensions in the appendix), ablations over training latent ranges, backbone (CLIP vs SigLIP), encoder size, and trained modalities, plus a candid analysis of failure cases and edge scenarios.

The ablation on training latent ranges (Figure 8) is informative, showing that the training noise distribution must be matched to the inference stage, and the finding that gains do not transfer cleanly from CLIP to SigLIP is honestly reported.

The central claim (50% denoising-step reduction at ~95-98% of full-cost VQAScore in BoN) is supported by the cost accounting in Section 5.2 and the results in Figures 4-5 and Tables 1-2, and the paper is written clearly enough to follow the argument end-to-end.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially CLIP image-encoder fine-tuning with InfoNCE on latents passed through a linear latent-to-RGB heuristic projection (cited to a blog post). Most of the value lies in the benchmark/datasets rather than a new algorithm; the paper is arguably closer to a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, which should be stated explicitly.

Missing quantitative comparison with the closest related work: latent CLIP of Becker et al. [3] and the online-feedback approach of Papalampidi et al. [30] are discussed in Related Work as the most similar efforts, but no head-to-head results against them are reported, weakening the claimed gap ('first to explore and benchmark').

Potential circularity in evaluation: training data is generated by SDXL from rewritten CC12M, and all evaluation images are also generated by SDXL with a fixed 50-step schedule; the linear projection Phi and the learned encoder may be tuned to this specific model/scheduler, and generalization to other diffusion models, samplers, or step counts is never tested.

Reliance on VQAScore as the sole ground-truth ranking metric raises consistency concerns: NoisyCLIP is trained to mimic a CLIP-style similarity space while being judged by VQAScore, and no human evaluation or alternative verifier (e.g., a stronger VLM judge) is used to confirm that the modest ~1-2% gains are meaningful.

Absolute gains are small and inconsistent across settings: ~1% improvement over baselines in many BoN plots, and the SigLIP backbone does not inherit the latent-alignment gains (R@1 0.194 vs 0.506), suggesting the approach may be sensitive to the pre-trained representation rather than a general technique.

Some experimental details are under-specified: the 'fixed latent interval (20-29)' is introduced without justification until much later, the relation between the 50k training latents and the two datasets is confusingly described, and typos/grammar issues (e.g., 'Bussiness Card', 'genetation', agreement errors) appear throughout, indicating insufficient polish.

No discussion of limitations beyond generation (e.g., behavior under guidance rescaling, flow-matching models, or latent spaces with different channel statistics), and the societal-impact discussion is absent, though the topic (compute efficiency) is relatively low-risk.

strengths: The problem is relevant and practically motivated: early detection of prompt misalignment during reverse diffusion could genuinely reduce the compute wasted in Best-of-N selection pipelines.

The paper introduces two released benchmark datasets (Noisy-Conceptual-Captions and Noisy-GenAI-Bench) containing intermediate latent sequences, addressing a real reproducibility gap the authors convincingly argue exists.

Experimental coverage is fairly broad for the claims made: language-to-latent alignment over denoising steps, Best-of-N trade-off curves, a factual-consistency task, ablations over training latent ranges (Fig. 8), trained encoders, model size, and a second backbone (SigLIP), plus honest failure-case analysis in the appendix.

The paper is generally well written, the method (freezing the text encoder shared with the diffusion model and fine-tuning only the image encoder with InfoNCE) is clearly described, and the discussion of known CLIP limitations transferring to the latent space (negation, counting) is candid.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core method is a straightforward fine-tuning of a pretrained CLIP image encoder on linearly projected noisy latents with InfoNCE. Prior work the authors themselves cite (latent CLIP [3]; dynamic CFG via online latent feedback [30]) already scores latents during diffusion; the claimed 'first' contributions rest mainly on the absence of a dedicated benchmark, which weakens the framing.

A critical missing baseline: decoding intermediate latents with the VAE decoder and applying frozen CLIP (or VQAScore) at intermediate steps. The paper replaces the decoder with a cheap linear projection (citing a blog post [47]) but never quantifies the accuracy gap versus the proper decoding baseline, nor the wall-clock cost trade-off. Since the entire contribution hinges on the linear projection being a good approximation, this comparison is essential and its absence is hard to justify.

Gains are modest and evaluation is partly circular. The reference ranking in Sec. 5.1 is defined by VQAScore, and BoN performance is also measured with VQAScore, so NoisyCLIP is partly optimized toward reproducing a score from the same family. Absolute improvements are small (e.g., ~1-1.7% VQAScore over mid-generation CLIP; 0.709 vs 0.747 for the final-image baseline), and the headline '50% cost for 98% performance' framing presents a 2% drop favorably.

Fragile generalization: (i) all training and evaluation is on a single generator (SDXL) with a single sampler/schedule, so applicability to other diffusion models is untested; (ii) the SigLIP variant (NoisySigLIP) fails to transfer the latent-alignment gains (R@1 0.194 vs 0.506), suggesting the improvement is not a general property of the recipe but partly backbone-specific; (iii) training on SDXL-generated images and testing on SDXL-generated images risks distribution match that real user pipelines would not have.

Cost accounting is incomplete. The reported savings count only diffusion steps and ignore the recurring cost of running NoisyCLIP at every (or many) intermediate steps, the memory cost of maintaining N parallel trajectories (the 'only one image proceeds' policy still requires batching N denoising processes, which many production systems cannot do), and alternative savings strategies (e.g., simply using fewer steps, or early-exit/step-skipping methods) that are not compared.

Several presentation and rigor issues: inconsistent citations for SDXL ([35] vs [40]); the choice of the fixed latent interval 20-29 is asserted as 'validated in Section 5.4.1' before its justification appears; the 'dataset' contributions are essentially prompt sets plus cached latents from one generator, which limits long-term benchmark value; and no human evaluation corroborates the VQAScore-based conclusions.

For an Algorithms/General contribution, the evidence supports 'it works a bit, in one setting' rather than a substantive advance: the deltas over a reasonably configured mid-generation CLIP baseline are within the range one would want to see backed by significance testing, which is not reported.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practical problem: alignment assessment currently requires waiting for full denoising, which is wasteful in Best-of-N regimes. The motivation for in-process (latent-space) alignment scoring is convincing and timely.

The proposed method is well-motivated and cleanly executed: fine-tuning only the image encoder of a frozen-CLIP twin-tower on SDXL-generated noisy latents preserves consistency with the diffusion model's text conditioning space. This is a sensible and reproducible design choice, supported by an ablation (Table 4) showing image-encoder-only training is the right choice.

The paper makes a datasets/benchmarks contribution in addition to the method: two open datasets (Noisy-Conceptual-Captions, Noisy-GenAI-Bench) containing latent sequences, which addresses a real reproducibility gap the authors convincingly argue (no standardized noisy-latent data exists). This could benefit follow-up work regardless of the specific method.

The experimental campaign is broad: alignment-through-denoising analysis (Fig. 3), cost-aware BoN trade-off analysis (Fig. 4-5), factual consistency with targeted non-factual prompt corruption (Fig. 7, Appendix A), backbone transfer (SigLIP), training-range ablations (Fig. 8), model-size scaling (Table 5), and an unusually honest qualitative failure-case analysis (Appendix F).

The headline claims are stated with appropriate calibration: 50% compute reduction at ~98% of final-image VQAScore, and per-skill gains of ~1-4%, are modest but consistently reported rather than oversold.
weaknesses: Scope of generalization is narrow relative to the framing as a general framework. All training and evaluation is on SDXL with its specific 4-channel latent space and linear latent-to-RGB mapping (citing a blog post, [47]). It is unclear whether NoisyCLIP transfers to other diffusion backbones (SD 1.5/3, FLUX, pixel-space diffusion) or other samplers/schedules. The SigLIP result (NoisySigLIP lagging by 2.6x in R@1) further suggests the gains may not even transfer across contrastive backbones, which the authors acknowledge but do not explain.

The absolute effect sizes are small in several key experiments: ~1% VQAScore improvement over frozen CLIP at matched cost (Fig. 5), and ~1.6-1.7% average gap-to-final improvement (Table 2). No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance across seeds are reported, so it is hard to judge whether these margins are robust, particularly given VQAScore noise.

Potential circularity in evaluation: VQAScore is used both to define the reference ranking of candidate images (Sec. 5.1) and as the primary success metric. No human evaluation is provided to validate that VQAScore-selected images are genuinely preferred, and Appendix A relies on LLM-generated (Gemma 3) corruptions whose quality is itself unverified by humans.

Training data is entirely self-generated by SDXL from CC12M rewrites, meaning the encoder may learn SDXL-specific artifacts rather than general noisy-image semantics; the paper does not discuss this potential bias or the risk of training/evaluation set overlap in style and failure modes.

The relation to closely related work could be sharper: latent-CLIP [3] and dynamic CFG via online feedback [30] are related in spirit, and the 'first to apply early stopping in BoN' claim would benefit from more careful delineation. Minor issues also hurt polish: typos ('genetation', 'missalignments', 'Bussiness'), inconsistent citation of SDXL as both [35] and [40] in Section 4.5, and a missing explicit limitations/societal-impact discussion in the main text.

Several numbers are hard to reconcile across sections (e.g., 0.85 vs 0.84 baseline VQAScore for the same N=6 setting in Sec. 5.2 vs Fig. 5 discussion), and some claims ('achieving 98% of CLIP performance' in the abstract) mix baselines in ways that require careful reader reconciliation.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the paper identifies a genuine gap—assessing text alignment during (rather than after) reverse diffusion—and articulates why post-hoc evaluation wastes compute in Best-of-N regimes.

The proposed approach is technically sound and simple: fine-tuning the CLIP image encoder with InfoNCE on noise-corrupted latents (interval 20-29) while freezing the text encoder, which keeps the diffusion conditioning space consistent. This design choice is justified and ablated.

Comprehensive empirical evidence: alignment-through-denoising analysis (Fig. 3), latent-to-text retrieval against targeted non-factual distractors, a systematic training-range ablation (Fig. 5), cost-normalized BoN comparisons against frozen CLIP/SigLIP and LatentCLIP variants, skill-level breakdowns (Appendix C), a small human preference study (61.3% preference, κ=0.724), and zero-shot generalization to two DiT architectures (SD3.5, FLUX.1).
Concrete practical payoff: ~50% reduction in denoising steps while matching or nearly matching full-cost frozen CLIP selection, with a sensible cost accounting scheme (denoising steps as the unit).

Contribution of reusable resources: two benchmark datasets with full latent sequences and a documented LLM-based corruption protocol for factual-consistency testing, addressing reproducibility gaps noted in prior latent-alignment work.
Honest limitations discussion: failure cases (negation, counting, attribute swapping), backbone-transfer caveats for SigLIP, and known CLIP biases transferring to the noisy setting.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the core technique is a standard contrastive fine-tune on synthetic noisy latents. Most of the value lies in the empirical study and data curation; reviewers expecting a new algorithmic contribution may find the method straightforward.

Potential evaluation circularity: both training data and the primary evaluation pipeline are built on SDXL-generated images, and reference rankings use VQAScore. NoisyCLIP may partly learn SDXL-specific latent statistics rather than general language-to-latent alignment; the claim of generalization to DiTs via VAE decoding only partially addresses this, since DiT latents are handled through a different decoding path than anything seen in training.

Benchmark scale is modest: Noisy-Conceptual-Captions (1000 captions) and Noisy-GenAI-Bench (1600 prompts, 10 generations each) are small; the human study covers only 100 pairs. Gains over strong baselines (LatentCLIP-4-plus) are sometimes within ~1-2 VQAScore points, and statistical significance/variance across seeds is not reported.

Verifier cost is not fully accounted: the cost model counts only denoising steps, ignoring the compute of scoring N noisy latents with a ViT-L encoder at intermediate checkpoints, which slightly flatters the reported savings.

No comparison against learned reward/verifier models (e.g., ImageReward, PickScore, HPS) as BoN selectors, which are natural strong baselines for this task even if they cannot run on latents directly.

The paper does not clearly commit to releasing models and code (datasets are described as open, but release status of NoisyCLIP weights and training data is ambiguous), which affects reproducibility of the central artifact.

Clarity issues in places: figure-heavy results with small fonts (Figs. 3-7), some inconsistent terminology ('perfomance', latent indexing conventions), and the claim of retaining '98% of post-hoc CLIP performance' varies depending on which baseline/split is referenced.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: early assessment of text-image alignment during reverse diffusion, motivated by the compute waste in Best-of-N test-time scaling. The framing of alignment assessment as a continuous in-process monitor rather than a post-hoc check is sensible and useful.

The contribution is well supported empirically for an applied/systems contribution: multiple evaluation tasks (alignment trajectory analysis, factual-consistency retrieval, early-stopping BoN), two new released-style benchmarks (Noisy-Conceptual-Captions, Noisy-GenAI-Bench) with intermediate latents, generalization tests on DiT-based architectures (SD3.5, FLUX.1) trained only on SDXL data, an encoder-size ablation, trained-modality ablation, failure-case analysis, and a small blind human preference study (61.3% preference, κ=0.724).

The training-range analysis (Section 5.2, Figure 5) is a genuinely useful empirical study: it shows how the choice of noisy-latent training range affects inference-stage performance and justifies the middle-range (20-29) choice.

Honest reporting in several places: the paper acknowledges that LatentCLIP is competitive in final-stage selection, that negation and universal-attribute prompts remain hard for all methods, and it discusses CLIP-inherited biases (counting, negation) transferring to the noisy latent setting.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is essentially contrastive fine-tuning of the CLIP image encoder on noise-corrupted latents with a frozen text encoder. This is a straightforward application of known techniques (InfoNCE, encoder fine-tuning) and is close to prior work the authors themselves cite (LatentCLIP [3], online-feedback CFG [32]). The claimed gap — 'dedicated analysis, open-source models, and standardized comparison data' — is primarily a dataset/benchmark contribution rather than an algorithmic one, and the paper would be better positioned if it declared that contribution type explicitly.

Marginal and possibly noise-level gains. Most reported improvements are 1-2% VQAScore differences (e.g., 0.85→0.86, '+2%' early-stage separation) with no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing. The headline claim of 'matches or beats frozen CLIP at full cost' is more accurately 'retains ~98% of performance at half cost', and the qualitative gains in Figure 8 are cherry-picked complex prompts.

Potential circularity in the main evaluation. VQAScore is used both to define the reference ranking of candidates (Section 5.1) and as the primary metric for selection quality (Sections 4.4, 5.3). Since the baselines are CLIP-style encoders being compared against a VQAScore-derived ground truth, the evaluation partially bakes in a preference for VQA-style semantic judgment; a human evaluation at scale or additional independent metrics would be needed to fully support the conclusions. The human study covers only 100 pairs from one split.

Unclear scoring overhead accounting. Cost is defined purely in diffusion steps, but the frequency of NoisyCLIP scoring during generation (and its cost relative to a diffusion step, especially for N candidates) is not specified. Without this, the claimed 50% compute saving is not fully verifiable, and early-scoring at multiple checkpoints could erode the savings.

Training data construction raises questions: only 50,000 latents from SDXL generations with LLM-rewritten CC12M captions. The model may latch onto SDXL-specific generation artifacts rather than genuine text-alignment signal; the zero-shot DiT transfer (+2%, +1.8%) via VAE decoding is encouraging but modest, and the reliance on a community blog post [48] for the latent-to-RGB linear transform is unusual for a reproducibility-focused contribution.

Mixed baseline results weaken the headline story: LatentCLIP beats NoisyCLIP on final-image selection (0.764 vs. 0.709 BoN; LatentCLIP-4-Plus is best in most Table 2/3 final-image columns), so the advantage is confined to the mid-generation regime. This is a fair but narrower claim than the abstract implies, and the value of that regime depends on how often practitioners need sub-50-step early stopping rather than simply using fewer steps or distillation.

Writing and presentation issues: inconsistent notation (latent index vs. 'denoising step' vs. 'latent position' used interchangeably; Table 1 'it. 21-30' vs. text 'latent 20'), small figures with hard-to-read axes (Figs. 3, 4, 6), and several claims stated without supporting numbers in the main text. No explicit limitations section or societal-impact discussion; release of models/datasets is implied but not clearly committed.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: evaluating prompt-latent alignment during the reverse diffusion process to enable early termination of unpromising trajectories in Best-of-N sampling, rather than only post-hoc assessment of final images.

NoisyCLIP is a simple, well-motivated approach (contrastive fine-tuning of the image encoder on noise-corrupted latents with a frozen text encoder shared with the diffusion conditioning space), making it easy to reproduce and adopt.

The paper introduces two new benchmark datasets (Noisy-Conceptual-Captions, Noisy-GenAI-Bench) with full latent sequences and targeted non-factual prompt corruptions, addressing a real gap in standardized evaluation resources for intermediate diffusion representations.

Evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: multiple tasks (alignment estimation, latent-to-text retrieval, early-stopping BoN), multiple baselines (CLIP, SigLIP, LatentCLIP variants), multiple architectures (SDXL, SD3.5, FLUX.1), and extensive ablations in the appendix (trained encoders, encoder size, training latent ranges, per-skill analysis, human evaluation with κ=0.724).
Failure case analysis and qualitative examples are candid and informative, and the observed generalization to DiT architectures (without retraining) is a valuable robustness result.

The practical outcome is concrete and quantified: up to 50% reduction in denoising steps with ~2% VQAScore drop, and up to 2% latent-selection improvement at latent 20 where all baselines degenerate to random selection.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in evaluation: VQAScore is used both to establish the reference ranking of images and as the primary metric for evaluating how well NoisyCLIP selects images. Since VQAScore itself has known biases, the reported gains partly measure agreement with this proxy rather than true alignment; human evaluation (100 pairs) is a good supplement but small.

Magnitude of improvements is modest in absolute terms (typically 1-3% across tables), and on some advanced skills (e.g., negation) all methods including NoisyCLIP perform poorly; the paper should be more careful distinguishing statistically meaningful gains.

The zero-shot generalization claim for DiT architectures is under-explained: NoisyCLIP is trained on linear-RGB-decoded SDXL latents (citing a blog post for the transformation), yet is applied to VAE-decoded latents of SD3.5/FLUX.1, a substantially different input distribution. The +2%/+1.8% gains in this setting deserve a deeper analysis of why such transfer works, given how different the two latent decoding schemes are.

The cost accounting is simplified: it counts only denoising steps and ignores the compute overhead of scoring N candidates with a ViT-L encoder at intermediate steps, as well as the cost of generating the SDXL training data (50k latents). The effective compute savings are therefore somewhat overstated.

Some inconsistencies and clarity issues: the abstract claims NoisyCLIP 'at half cost matches or beats frozen CLIP at full cost' while the results section reports a ~2% drop at half cost; the latent interval notation (e.g., 'latent 20', 'iteration 21-30', 'latent position') is used inconsistently across sections and figures; and Table 1 reports R@1 for final-image models as undefined without explanation.

The training data and benchmarks are exclusively derived from SDXL generations and CC12M-rewritten captions, raising questions about style/generator bias of the learned scorer, which is only partially addressed by the zero-shot DiT experiments.

No explicit limitations or societal impact discussion; the ethical considerations of large-scale synthetic training data are not addressed, though dataset derivation and attribution are otherwise clearly documented.
